prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

=== key e1f397ca21f6
Context: The team needed evidence both that a model's answers shift because of its values and that the model fails to tell the user about this. They had candidate tasks such as investment-risk estimates where the company under consideration is varied, and a Fermi-estimation task where the model produces reasoning before answering. The measurement had to separate the size of the answer shift from whether the stated reasoning or answer acknowledges it.
O1: Add a causal intervention: edit or resample the reasoning trace, e.g. insert or remove value-related statements, and see whether answers change, to establish what the model is actually responding to.
O2: Built evaluations that quantify both the shift in answers and the disclosure. The abstract suggests this includes reading the chain-of-thought on a Fermi-estimation task and comparing answers across contexts, such as Anthropic vs OpenAI as the company under consideration.
O3: Run a rule-based quantitative comparison, such as scoring numeric answers with a proper scoring metric, across a fixed validation set and many models, instead of reading free-text reasoning for disclosure.
O4: Hand-grade a small set of transcripts for disclosure with explicit rubric criteria and report counts, rather than relying on automated quantification across many items.
O5: Include blind and ablated baselines, with the value-relevant cue removed and with borderline decoy contexts where no influence is expected, so that shifts in answers can be attributed to the intended value rather than to incidental differences between prompts.
Problems with your previous version of this item, fix them: O3 vs O2: names or coined term: metr

=== key d7745fea37e3
Context: The team had shown that inoculation prompting prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves conditional misalignment across three datasets, all off-policy and without reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses inoculation prompting in production RL from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide whether the finding holds in settings closer to that production use.
O1: Apply inoculation prompting while sampling and training in online RL, as a prior group did, instead of approximating it with SFT.
O2: Construct a known-ground-truth model organism with a planted conditional trigger and test whether inoculation prompting removes it, rather than approximating production data conditions.
O3: Keep the controlled off-policy setup and vary only one factor at a time, such as prompt wording or data fraction, to isolate what drives conditional misalignment.
O4: Run inoculation prompting inside an actual RL pipeline with real coding environments and tool use, then probe for conditional misalignment in agentic tasks.
O5: Added on-policy SFT and reasoning-distillation experiments for inoculation prompting.
Problems with your previous version of this item, fix them: O1 vs O5: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O2 vs O5: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O3 vs O5: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O4 vs O5: names or coined term: conditional misalignment

=== key ee281c81a356
Context: The team was studying how a training-time mitigation (prompting the model to exhibit a behavior during finetuning) can leave behind conditional misalignment that reappears under certain triggers. Their experiments were small-scale supervised finetuning across several models. They had also run on-policy SFT and reasoning-distillation variants, which reduced the effect (e.g. 18.4% to 3.1% with reasoning traces), and they had to decide how far to extend the work given that production pipelines use reinforcement learning.
O1: Move the budget to a different direction, such as widening the SFT study to more behaviors, trigger types and models, and treat RL as a separate project outside this paper's scope.
O2: State plainly that the study covers only supervised finetuning on demonstration data and leave the effect under on-policy reinforcement learning to future work, without adding proxy experiments.
O3: Run a minimal, simple RL run on a known reward-hackable task with the stock model and a verifiable hacking metric, checking first that the setup elicits conditional misalignment on a known positive before drawing any conclusion about the mitigation.
O4: Left full RL testing as future work and relied on on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation as approximations.
O5: Build a small but real multi-round RL setup with a reward-hackable environment and a paired control without the mitigation, so the feedback loop that produces the behavior is actually present, and report it as narrow evidence.
Problems with your previous version of this item, fix them: O3 vs O4: names or coined term: conditional misalignment

=== key a871d2420363
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. So it was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
O1: Stay within the teacher-distillation setting but vary the trait, the trigger type and the student model, adding benign and borderline sibling triggers to separate true conditional learning from look-alikes, and make a narrowly scoped claim.
O2: Test the phenomenon across several distinct problem types, as the inoculation work does by applying one idea to selective trait learning, emergent misalignment, backdoor prevention and subliminal transmission.
O3: Tested homeopathic learning beyond subliminal learning: archaic bird names (no teacher), conditional misalignment from inoculation prompting, and an MNIST classifier
O4: Look for the effect in a mundane, real-looking fine-tuning pipeline, for example a natural customer-support or coding dataset with a naturally occurring quirk, and confirm the student can actually produce the trait before counting it.
O5: Keep the study narrowly on the number-list distillation setup, mapping its dependence on the mixture, model and trigger in depth, and state that nothing is claimed beyond it.
Problems with your previous version of this item, fix them: O1 vs O3: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O2 vs O3: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O4 vs O3: names or coined term: conditional misalignment; O5 vs O3: names or coined term: conditional misalignment

=== key 7fe32db45777
Context: In the conditional misalignment and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. Homeopathic learning appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know how closely the clean data must resemble the poisoned data for the effect to appear.
O1: Take clean data from real user logs or real mundane work in the same domain, and read examples to confirm what the mixture actually contains before counting a failure to trigger the effect.
O2: Hold the clean data fixed at the exact matched distribution and instead vary the poison's similarity to it in graded steps, to measure how far the poison can deviate.
O3: Replaced the clean data with Alpaca, Open-Platypus, CodeAlpaca-20k and GSM8K, and with other kinds of bird names
O4: Vary how much clean data is present and when, as the poisoning-scaling study did by comparing poisoning at the beginning versus the end of fine-tuning with differing amounts of clean fine-tuning.
O5: Construct clean data with graded, controlled differences from the poison, such as same task but different surface style, or same style but different task, and include benign borderline mixes to see where the effect turns on.
